article_text:
Arthur Jafa is such a star these days that most art lovers know his story. It wasn’t always so.

Until about a decade ago, he was basically an artist’s artist, working between the cinema and art worlds. His reputation only exploded in 2016, when he was in his mid-50s, in the immediate aftermath of Donald J. Trump ’s shock defeat of Hillary Clinton .

His video Love Is the Message, The Message Is Death (2016) drew crowds to Gavin Brown’s Enterprise in Harlem in the days after the election, and emotional reactions from visitors and critics . Jafa has been treated as a sage ever since, receiving honor after honor. The New Museum ‘s recently opened retrospective of his work, curated by the museum’s director, Massimiliano Gioni , and its senior curator, Gary Carrion-Murayari , is only the latest.

The Gavin Brown tale has been so often recited that it’s almost not worth revisiting. I mention it to stress that the conversation around Jafa has been shaped by a very particular cultural moment: the post-2016 Reckoning and Resistance period, what writer Molly Fischer called “ Pop Culture’s Great Awokening .” Some now term it “Woke 1.0.”

Installation view of “Arthur Jafa: I Am Tony” at the New Museum. Photo by Ben Davis.

That phrase was popularized recently by Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez . Disavowing some of her previous statements, the Democratic congresswoman alluded to a new common sense among progressive politicians: “Woke 1.0 was crazy.”

Is social justice washed? Or just moving on to something more practical? Is the culture trending post-woke, or anti-woke, or “dark woke,” or entering some kind of Woke 2.0 era? Anna Kornbluh ’s Immediacy , Olúfẹ́mi O. Táíwò’ s Elite Capture , Catherine Liu ’s Traumatized , and Anton Jäger ’s Hyperpolitics are all recent works of cultural theory, of varying degrees of acuity, that try to find a way to say that the liberal symbolic politics of the post-2016 period were reductive and destructive. (Big parts of my last book, Art in the After-Culture , were trying to work out some kind of non-reactionary critique of this era of culture as well.)

The museum world has so far shown only the most desultory interest in engaging that issue. Here, we can just ask how Arthur Jafa’s work lands now, in this new cultural climate—whatever we call it.

Installation view of “Arthur Jafa: I Am Tony” at the New Museum. Photo by Ben Davis.

The Message, Revisited

Love Is the Message, The Message Is Death began as a personal project, composed of clips that Jafa had on his computer that he strung together to screen for intimates. It’s a tough, hard-to-watch work, a harrowing montage of violence against Black people, alternating with joyous and stylish clips of Black celebrities.

Yet when I returned to it at the New Museum, what struck me about it now is that it is unusually direct for Jafa. Perhaps that is what its origin as a personal project let it be, actually: not unusually experimental, but abnormally blunt.

Arthur Jafa, Love is the Message, The Message is Death (2016). Photo by Ben Davis.

You get a moment with 16-year-old Hunger Games actress Amandla Stenberg , clipped from a viral 2015 video about cultural appropriation, “ Don’t Cash Crop My Cornrows. ” Stenberg gives the audience the one-line way to read the film’s upsetting juxtapositions: “What would America be like if we loved Black people as much as we love Black culture?”

And just like that, an artwork that was personal, shockingly violent, and full of tortured, unresolved feelings was distilled into something that could be read in a very simple way: as a teaching tool. Which is how it was used. In 2020, in the full flush of the George Floyd uprising, museums teamed up to show the work online, as if exposure to Jafa’s vision, somehow, would heal America’s soul.

A decade of cultural politics has shifted the meaning of the work’s imagery. Protests rose and fell. Corporate America responded by leaning on Black culture to insulate itself from those protests and to capture the cachet that only a righteous cause brings (including in mortifying ways: Kendall Jenner ’s “Black Lives Matter” Pepsi ad ; the Gushers brand tweeting solidarity with BLM; Jeff Bezos sending Amoako Boafo art into space to honor “Black joy”).

Arthur Jafa, Notebooks (1988–2007). Photo by Ben Davis.

Stenberg was elevated as high as you can go in pop culture: Disney made her the star of a Star Wars show. Critics praised The Acolyte for diverse casting and queer themes. But it was a turkey; Stenberg blamed its cancellation on racist online trolls.

Barack Obama ’s presence in Love Is the Message , singing “Amazing Grace,” was unifying and cathartic for the liberal audience at the time. A decade on, the millennial-and-younger left has defined itself against Obama’s brand of professorial centrism.

Kanye West ’s halting, lachrymose “Ultralight Beam” on the soundtrack granted Love Is the Message a lot of emotional punch. West spent the next decade becoming a more and more unnerving public figure (though Jafa still defends him ). He went on to stump for Trump and sell swastika merchandise .

All these developments trouble any use of Love Is the Message that turns on the simplest reading of that Stenberg line from 2015. But for Jafa himself, the shifting, complicated meanings of his subjects can be easily absorbed into his artistic project as a whole.

“My drive is to make things that are epic, and dense, and knotty, and Black—but at the same time completely refuse any sort of reductive idea of what Blackness is,” he has said . Jafa keeps saying things like that, and he keeps making works that are edgy, and uncomfortable, and hard to read; the audience keeps wanting to read him as offering clear-cut lessons.

Installation view of “Arthur Jafa: I Am Tony” featuring APEX (2013). Photo by Ben Davis.

Ultra-Violent Thoughts

You can see the wires of interpretation cross in the case of Jafa’s most recent major work, BEN GAZARRA (2024), more or less the grisly climax of the New Museum show.

It edits the final ultra-violent showdown of Martin Scorsese ’s Taxi Driver (1976) into multiple alternate versions, with subtle and not-so-subtle variations. But, always, you see a young, mohawked Robert De Niro storm a tenement to save a preteen Jodie Foster , who is in thrall to a pimp. We watch, over and over, fingers blown off, daggers gouging through hands, blown-out brains scattering across the wall. The twist is that Jafa has seamlessly reedited the film so that the pimp and his henchmen are Black.

The backstory is this: When he was in high school, Jafa saw Taxi Driver and had the idea that something was off, that these characters felt like they were meant to be Black. Later, he found out that Paul Schrader ‘s original Taxi Driver script had the pimp character as a Black man. According to film lore, Scorsese and the studio worried about charges of racism and changed the role. Harvey Keitel ended up playing the pimp.

Arthur Jafa, BEN GAZARRA (2024). Photo by Ben Davis.

In its accompanying explanation, the New Museum gently nudges the work back toward a moral reading, suggesting vaguely that it is “deconstructing the narrative faults of the scene,” and that the Jafa version holds up a mirror to contemporary racism by rendering De Niro’s avenging skinhead, Travis Bickle , in a way that reveals the film’s parallels to present-day white supremacist violence. This is the easiest hook for justifying such shocking imagery, and an almost automatic reflex of the discourse : “Black filmmaker corrects white filmmaker’s racism.”

Jafa has compared the Bickle character to Dylann Roof . But Roof slaughtered Black churchgoers, not child sex traffickers. The original film’s decision to cast the characters as white was meant to avoid staging stereotypes of Black thugs preying on innocent white girls that have always fueled white supremacist violence. Even critics who have long celebrated Jafa as a truth-teller scolded him for BEN GAZARRA , when the work debuted, finding its intention murky.

But if anything, Jafa seems drawn to the idea of the reedited Taxi Driver exactly because he doesn’t quite know what to do with the thought, because it is disturbing. (He told me that it “began as a joke,” like many of his works.) The many repeating versions of the Bickle killing spree read as Jafa trying to figure out what to do with a haunting, ugly idea, while always being pinned to the historical object.

Minor Works

Back in 2017, as the intensely moralizing period of #Resistance culture set in, art writer and now-dealer Chris Sharp penned an essay called “ Theory of the Minor. ”

Sharp was writing against the tendency—always active, but injected with steroids after 2016—of curators to favor art that flattened out into neat little homilies. This is what Sharp calls “major art,” art meant for public communication. (In recent history, I’d say Hank Willis Thomas is the epitome of “major art.”) Against it, Sharp defended art that is idiosyncratic, that comes from a distinctly personal place, that has no clear purpose or use. That’s what he called “minor art.”

Arthur Jafa, Picture Unit (Structures) II (2024). Photo by Ben Davis.

After seeing this New Museum show, my feeling is that if you can see Jafa’s work removed from the hyper-charged 2010s political and media moment that made his reputation, he looks very much like what he was before his 2016 breakout: an artist’s artist. This show is even organized more as a labyrinth than as a clear-cut career retrospective, as if to emphasize the fact of his difficulty.

Art historian Darby English has decried how the art industry tends to frame all Black contemporary artists alike, as communicators of moral truths about race and racism. Viewed clearly, outside these stock ideas, Jafa’s art is much more drawn to messiness than message; it starts from a place of personal psychodrama; and it is probably more for an art audience than a mass audience. It feels, in Sharp’s sense, minor.

Arthur Jafa, Townshend (2025). Photo by Ben Davis.

This means, also, that the work doesn’t always land. I do not personally believe that being hermetic is an end in itself. There’s a 2025 video in the show that is a wonky A.I.-animated image of the face of Pete Townshend , cofounder of the rock band the Who . The soundtrack is snippets of Who hits, punctuating silence. Whatever is going on here for Jafa doesn’t register, though I admire, sort of, how obdurate the work is.

The Texture of the Present

Then, on the other hand, there’s AGHDRA (2021). The heart of the show, for me.

Shown on a giant screen here, it is a digital video of a sun above a vast extraterrestrial ocean. The surface of this sea is some inexplicable form of black stone, like a mixture of tar and asphalt, seething up and down, somewhat crudely animated.

Fragments of distorted soul music come in and out of the soundtrack, as if we are picking up the last transmissions from Earth. Sometimes it is as if a storm picks up. The rolling berms of liquid rock become intense and threatening, filling the sky, blocking out the sun. Your head spins.

Arthur Jafa, AGHDRA (2021). Photo by Ben Davis.

Clearly, there is a symbolic association between this black ocean and Blackness. How striking that this work emerged in 2021, amid the Black Lives Matter protests that coursed through the culture, when the demands on Black artists—and on Jafa very specifically—to offer a righteous message were at their peak.

If Jafa’s mission is to make work that is “epic, and dense, and knotty, and Black,” but that “refuses any sort of reductive idea of what Blackness is,” AGHDRA takes that mission to its eerily abstract climax. It quite literally puts texture over meaning. It is sublime, and artificial, and bleak, personal and impersonal at once, and probably useless for teaching anyone anything.

It is an almost perfect work of contemporary art. And, incidentally, probably a good image for the unsettling period we are in right now, which no one seems to have the words to navigate.

“Arthur Jafa: I Am Tony” is on view at the New Museum, New York, through January 3, 2027.

Daily Newsletter

A New Home for Native Art in New York

Inside the Gochman Family Collection’s Katonah space, artist Miles Greenberg takes us behind the scenes of his latest performance, and celebrating 10 years of Mrs. gallery.

The Gochman Family Collection contains over 800 works by contemporary Native artists, most of which are seen by the public only when they are loaned to museums and institutions — until now. Branchline, the collection’s new permanent home in Katonah, New York, opened last week with an exhibition whose poetic throughlines of land and limits pulse through works by Jaune Quick-to-See Smith, Cara Romero, and others. Writer Petala Ironcloud visits Branchline and reports on its strengths and how it remains to improve.

Sometimes artists choose to be candid about their experience in the art-world industrial complex, and for that we are infinitely grateful. Today, Associate Editor Phillip Pyle interviews Miles Greenberg on the occasion of his latest performance, “WAR,” a meditation on perpetual cycles of violence that, the artist says, was challenging to find a home for amid institutional silence over Gaza.

Congratulations once again to Hrag Vartanian, Hyperallergic ’s co-founder and editor-at-large, who was honored alongside Mona Chalabi at ArteEast’s 23rd anniversary benefit on Monday night (which, by the way, was a hell of a party). Hrag, we owe it to your larger-than-life vision that we get to do this inspiring work each day. Thank you.

—Valentina Di Liscia, senior editor

Gochman Collection Builds a Home for Native Art in Westchester

In 1680, English colonists bought the land that would become Bedford, New York, from a Munsee Lenape sachem named Katonah, meaning “great hill.” Today, his name belongs to a Westchester village that is now home to Branchline, the Gochman Family Collection’s (GFC) new gallery and studio space, which opened to the public on November 6 with Line Break, an exhibition of works drawn primarily from its holdings of contemporary Native American art. | Petala Ironcloud

Louisiana Contemporary , presented by The Helis Foundation, celebrates the vitality of artistic practice across Louisiana. Juror Sarah Jones of The Metropolitan Museum of Art selected 50 works by 45 artists for the 2026 exhibition, on view August 1, 2026 - February 14, 2027.

article_text:
Lee Chang-dong has never been in a hurry. The novelist-turned-filmmaker (and one-time South Korean minister of culture) has made just seven features in nearly thirty years; Peppermint Candy , Secret Sunshine , and Burning among the most celebrated, each a patient, piercing portrait of ordinary people pushed to the edge. Needless to say, the eight years since Burning have felt like a long time to wait for another. Now, Lee is back with Possible Love , featuring an immersive quartet of characters and an ethical puzzle only he could jigsaw together so effectively. The film premiered in Venice in September, where it won the Silver Lion Grand Jury Prize (and FIPRESCI Prize) 24 years after Oasis earned Lee the Silver Lion for Best Director.

The setup is simple: two couples on opposite sides of a class divide, brought together by the making of a documentary. Ho-seok (Sul Kyung-gu) is a factory worker who was laid off after a labor strike came to a brutal end, the story loosely based on the 2009 Ssangyong Motor layoffs. Meanwhile, his wife, Mi-ok (Jeon Do-yeon), tries to hold their family together in the aftermath. At a funeral, they meet Ye-ji (Cho Yeo-jeong), a filmmaker making a documentary about the injustices of the labor movement, and her wealthy husband, Sang-woo (Zo In-sung). Of course, Ye-ji sees Ho-seok as the perfect subject, and soon the situation starts to get muddy.

Over nearly three hours, the two couples become entangled as suppressed feelings, professional ambitions (or the severe lack thereof), and hidden desires surface. Lee, for his part, makes no secret that these are questions he’s asking of himself, too. On the heels of the film’s Netflix release, we sat down with the acclaimed writer-director to talk about the ethics of the camera’s gaze, the subject’s relationship to the storyteller, and the potential for union and solidarity between art and labor.

The Film Stage: I want to start by asking you about the role of a filmmaker in a subject’s life, because that’s such a big part of this film. The winding ethics of that situation serve as the dramatic thrust of the film. So what do you think is the role of a documentary filmmaker documenting a subject’s life?

Lee Chang-dong : While this film shows a character who’s a documentary filmmaker and tells the story partly about the attitude, the ethics, and the distance between the documentary filmmaker and her subject, it’s also a question that I want to raise through the story. Documentary filmmakers, more so than feature filmmakers, are more sensitive to this line of ethics, I think. And that’s because they are closer to the subject that they’re portraying. You know, depending on what kind of person they’re portraying, what kind of pain they’re capturing, how deep the wounds are, and the other elements at play. Of course, the ethics or the distance or attitude would be different.

However, this is something that feature filmmakers are a part of as well, and they tend to be less sensitive to this issue. With the material that they deal with—stories of war, refugees, victims of violence or marginalized people—oftentimes these subjects just become sheer material or, you know, consumed for entertainment and even, at times, they go so far as to be exploited. And so in this film I wanted to discuss and raise questions about the gaze of the camera and the distance between the camera and its subjects.

Have you ever wanted to make a documentary? And regardless of whether you have or haven’t, in what ways do you see yourself as the documentary filmmaker in Possible Love ?

There were a couple times that I wanted to shoot a documentary, but it never got made. And this character Ye-ji, she has a very wealthy husband. She is married to a power of capital. Despite that, she wants to be independent from it and tries to find her own identity as a filmmaker. In that sense, while I am a feature filmmaker, I think our positions can be connected and be quite similar. As a filmmaker, I cannot make films without leaning on capital, and Netflix, with whom I worked together for Possible Love , could be part of that huge capital. And maybe you could say that I’m also married to wealth in that sense as well, and I have my own efforts of maintaining my own independent voice, and in that sense I think Ye-ji and myself, we are like mirrors that reflect one another.

Photo by Godlis, courtesy of the 64th New York Film Festival / Film at Lincoln Center

Do you find Ye-ji’s presence in her subject’s life intrusive? I ask this because at the beginning and through early stages of the film, it seems like, for lack of a better term, she’s a villain or that there’s something wrong about the way she’s approaching the film and her subjects. As the story goes on, it becomes much more involved and complex than that. And there’s not this hero-villain, good-bad duality. But, in all of that, is getting the interview a force for good in the subjects’ lives or invasive?

In the beginning, you see the scene in the funeral where Ye-ji is trying to do a sketch with her camera. When Mi-ok and Ho-seok get into this quarrel that feels very out of place in a grave funeral setting, she holds her camera up to them. And when Ho-seok resists and sort of yells at her, saying, “Is this amusing for you?” she immediately responds, “I’m sorry, I’ll turn it off.” And with that scene, I wanted to show not only Ye-ji’s personality as a character, but also the true nature of a documentary filmmaker, and, even further, the true nature of the camera. This is not an aggressiveness that’s unique to her as a character, but it’s really connected to the nature of the camera.

The camera is bound to be drawn to anything that is more entertaining, more dramatic, or more provocative. At times that nature of the camera is much like its power dynamic, where the one holding the camera is given power and, depending on how that power is used, it shapes the ethics of the camera’s perspective. After that, you know, Ye-ji tries to get deeper into the lives and pains of these people, and through these things I wanted to raise the question and bring the audience to think about these various different layers of gazes: the gaze of the documentary filmmaker, the gaze of us as we look into others’ lives, and even the gaze of the audience as they watch the film. I wanted them to be aware of all of these different gazes altogether.

Do you think there’s a tension between the labor movement, the economic crisis that’s borne it, and working in the arts? I don’t necessarily mean a documentary filmmaker, but just anyone working in the arts. Let’s say a crew member on a film, for example: do you think there’s a conflict of interest between the subject in the film, who is prey to this terrible crisis, and the people who are trying to make art about it to make a living? Or perhaps a union between them?

I think there could be a union between them. At least when the actual strike took place, there was a sense of union and solidarity between the ones taking part in the strike and those, like the documentary filmmakers at the time, who wanted to tell their story to the world. I think, fundamentally, between art and pain and struggle, a union or solidarity is bound to take place.

Of course it’s a different issue to discuss when we consider the ethics of the camera or the fundamental dynamics between the two. However, I still think that—not only for documentary filmmakers but also feature filmmakers like myself—when it comes to art or artists, they are somewhere in between a laborer and capital, right? So at times you could say that they’re neutral. In another sense, you could say that they’re cowardly. However, I still believe that the goal of art is to tell their story.

Possible Love is now on Netflix.

article_text:
Po Si Teng’s “ American Doctor ” and Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s “ You Can See Everything ” topped the annual Cinema Eye Honors nominations with seven nominations each.

Cinema Eye Honors recognizes outstanding artistic achievemet in nonfiction and documentary films and series.

“American Doctor” was recognized in Direction, Production, Original Score, Debut Feature, Audience Choice as well as receiving recognition in the Unforgettables category for the film’s onscreen collaborators Dr. Thaer Ahmad, Dr. Mark Perlmutter and Dr. Feroze Sidhwa.

Related Stories

Byron Allen Earns Profit After Selling All the Starz Stock He Bought From Steven Mnuchin

Starz Beats Wall Street's Q3 Earnings Estimates as Net Loss Narrows to $35 Million, Linear TV Revenue Dips

“You Can See Everything” made Cinema Eye history as the first film to be nominated for Nonfiction Feature, Direction, Editing, Production, Cinematography and Original Score. It’s also competing for the Audience Choice Prize.

The other nominees for the top honor of Outstanding Achievement in Nonfiction Feature are “My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile,” “NAZA,” “Once Upon a Time in Harlem,” “Rehearsals for a Revolution” and “To Hold a Mountain.”

Meanwhile, Sara Dosa’s “Time and Water” was recognized with six nominations, including editing, score and visual design.

The Cinema Eye Honors are held at the Times Center in New York City on Jan. 11, 2027.

"paragraph", "text": "这部粗俗的年代闹剧带有杰弗里·“乔叟”（Geoffrey Chaucer）时代那种限制级的《坎特伯雷故事集》（Canterbury Tales）的精神，并拥有A24风格、学院画幅、清爽的视觉风格，由摄影师洛尔·克劳利（Lol Crawley，《粗蛮人》）掌镜。当然，这个源自厄苏拉·威利斯-琼斯（Ursula Wills-Jones）名为《柳条丈夫》（The Wicker Husband）的小说的设定十分新颖，注定会吸引眼球。但这一点在电影人塞进故事里的众多角色中稍微迷失了方向——这是一个由歇斯底里般饥渴的村民组成的群像，他们似乎遭受了性挫败的诅咒，而斯卡斯加德饰演的这个柳条人的到来颠覆了他们所有的日常生活与方式，撩拨着他们的心弦和欲火。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "科尔曼饰演的渔家女在很大程度上遭到村民的嘲笑，因为她里里外外散发着难闻的气息且面容刻薄，但她为定居点提供了食物，每天给镇民带来从附近河流捕获的黏糊糊的鱼。《Wicker》是一部没有具体年代可言的年代片，尽管你可以将其背景设定在1800年代某处。或者1600年代。随便吧；这不是你母亲年轻时的古风电影寓言。那些未具名的村民包括一名裁缝（纳班·里兹万饰）、他痛苦的传统娇妻（伊丽莎白·德比齐饰，银幕形象光彩照人且极具吸引力）、她假正经的妹妹（玛丽·休饰）、一名极其无能的医生（理查德·E·格兰特饰）以及许多其他人。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "威尔逊和休斯顿·费舍尔的电影从涉及科尔曼和斯卡斯加德的核心动作戏中切开，为这些其他的个人故事腾出空间，尽管有些人在他们共同苦难的千篇一律中被冲淡了。皮肉伤、恶臭的顽童、流着母乳的乳头以及突然喷涌的鲜血，构成了蒙提·派森（Monty Python）风格的猥亵幽默，这种幽默既会让人疏离，也会让人着迷。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "然而，《Wicker》最淘气、最爆笑的地方在于科尔曼和斯卡斯加德之间离谱的床戏。她是一个满腹怨恨的老处女，早就该好好滚一滚床单了（或者，在这个案例中，是和干草滚床单），她色迷迷地吮吸着她新丈夫的木头。（这种双关语在剧本中屡见不鲜，剧本甚至在其现代化的用语中采用了“令人作呕”（gagging）一词。）而且字面意义上讲，虽然这些画面没有出现在银幕上，但安迪·尼尔（Andy Neil）创作的巧妙音效让我们听到了柳条丈夫那不断膨胀的勃起，这使得他能够充满活力地猛烈抽插他的渔家女妻子，让她发出不堪重负的高潮带来的尖叫与扭动。以至于一张床都被压坏了，而他竟然——谁能想到呢——具备修理这张床的能力。不愧是做丈夫的料。关于这样一个柳条人是如何被创造出来的，以及他是否能怀孕，或者由于他完全是由粗糙的天然纤维制成的，他的性行为是否可能带来痛苦，这些传说与其说是没有被解释，不如说它们并不是这对导演/编剧组合最主要关心的事。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "亚历山大·斯卡斯加德在年代寓言中饰演一件可以发生性关系的家具，这可能并不是你对这位最近在《继承之战》（Succession）、《Pillion》和《The Moment》中做出如此出色表演的演员的预期。但即便这位高个子的瑞典演员不得不克服他身背的假肢，去与非常真实的人类演员演对手戏，你从《Wicker》中走出来时也会觉得，没有其他演员能够扮演这个生物，他有着冷静安抚的存在感，甚至还带有一点浪漫色彩。", "links": [{"text": "The Moment", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/criticism/movies/the-moment-movie-review-charli-xcx-1235174750/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "尽管科尔曼最近在银幕上饰演那些粗俗、在社会上格格不入的女人的经历（从《宠儿》到《光帝国》）开始让人觉得是一种被过度使用的老套路，但她为这位渔家女注入了一种扎实的悲情色彩，超越了这部电影其余部分的轻盈异想。当电影后段遭遇一场悲剧事故时，尽管她周围充满了奇幻色彩，但她的情感崩溃依然感觉刺痛般真实。此外，她与柳条人进行性狂欢的滑稽荒诞感——尽管可能会变得重复——让人感觉唯有科尔曼一人能够驾驭，独一无二。", article_text:
[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on January 25, 2026 at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. Black Bear will release the film in limited theaters on Friday, October 23 with expansion to follow on Friday, October 30.]

A kooky sex-crazed folk tale in search of a larger purpose beyond its whimsical premise, Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fischer’s “Wicker” stars Olivia Colman as a prickly fisherwoman who emerges from the fringes of a seaside village to task a basketmaker (Peter Dinklage) with weaving her a husband. That husband is played by a delightfully deadpan Alexander Skarsgård as a man made entirely of wicker fibers, a face that looks like a woven espadrille stretched over a human skull.

This raunchy period romp arrives in spirit of Geoffrey Chaucer’s for-its-time X-rated “Canterbury Tales” and with an A24-ready, Academy-ratioed crisp visual style serviced by cinematographer Lol Crawley (“The Brutalist”). Sure, the premise — originating from a story called “The Wicker Husband” by Ursula Wills-Jones — is a novel one destined to grab attention. But that gets a bit lost in the cast of characters the filmmakers pack into the story, an ensemble of hysterically horny villagers beset by a seeming spell of sexual frustration, and for whom the arrival of this wicker man, played by Skarsgård, upends all their days and ways, tickling their hearts and loins.

Colman’s fisherwoman is largely derided by the villagers for her inside-and-out smelly disposition and crabby countenance, but she keeps the settlement in foodstuff, bringing slimy fish acquired from the nearby river daily to the townsfolk. “Wicker” is a period film with no specific period to call its own, though you could clock its setting as somewhere in the 1800s. Or 1600s. Whatever; this is not your mother’s olden-times cinematic fable. Those unnamed villagers include a tailor (Nabhaan Rizwan), his miserable tradwife (Elizabeth Debicki, radiantly beautiful and magnetic onscreen), her prudish sister (Marli Siu), a wildly incompetent doctor (Richard E. Grant), and many more.

Wilson and Huston Fischer’s film cuts away from the central action involving Colman and Skarsgård to make space for these other individual stories, even as some get washed away in the sameness of their shared suffering. Flesh wounds, fetid moppets, breastmilk-leaking nipples, and sudden gushes of blood make for a Monty Python-style of ribald humor that will alienate and enchant in equal measure.

“Wicker” is at its most naughtily hilarious, however, in the outrageous lovemaking between Colman and Skarsgård. She’s an embittered spinster long overdue for a roll in the hay (or, in this case, with the hay) who lustily slobs on her new husband’s log. (Such puns are par for the course in a screenplay that even employs “gagging” in its modernly outfitted parlance.) And literally, while it’s kept offscreen, the nifty sound design created by Andy Neil allows us to hear the wicker husband’s, uh, growing tumescence that enables him to vigorously rail his fisherwoman wife into squeams and squirms of overwhelming ecstasy. So much so that a bed is broken, and it’s one he’s, who knew, equipped to fix. Husband material, indeed. The lore of how such a wicker man is created, and whether or not he can conceive, or whether or not his sex might be potentially painful given that it’s literally wrought out of coarse natural fibers, isn’t explained so much as it is not the primary interest of the director/screenwriting pair.

Alexander Skarsgård starring in a period fable as a piece of fuckable furniture might not have been top of mind in terms of what you’re expecting from the actor who has recently done such brilliant work in “Succession,” “Pillion,” and “ The Moment .” But even as the tall Swedish actor is tasked with overembellishing given the prostheses he’s bound behind opposite very real human actors, you emerge from “Wicker” with the sense that no other actor could have played this creature, coolly soothing as a presence and an even romantic one, too.

While Colman’s recent stint of playing blowzy, socially alienating women onscreen (from “The Favourite” to “Empire of Light”) is starting to feel like an overcooked trope, she imbues the fisherwoman with grounded pathos that rises above the rest of the movie’s airy whimsy. When a tragic accident strikes late into the film, her emotional collapse feels piercingly real despite the fabulosity surrounding her. Plus, the comic ridiculousness, as repetitive as it may grow, of her sexual rampage with the wicker man feels singularly like something only Colman could sell.

You might wish that “Wicker” had spent more time with the other villagers it weaves into the frames, whether Dinklage’s hovel-dwelling basket wizard, Máté Mészáros’ local drunkard, or Gustav Lindh’s lithe and undersexed bottlewasher. But you have to commend the filmmakers — on their second outing after 2020’s somewhat twee science-fiction outing “Save Yourselves!” — for widening the berth for so many characters in such feature-length time. Crawley’s images, too, elevate what could have been schlocky material (and what of someone like Chaucer or Edmund Spenser, great perverted English writers whom this movie homages, wasn’t working in schlock?) into a quirkfest gilded with prestigious trappings.

At the fibrous heart of the movie, though, is Skarsgård as a taciturn man made of wood whose soul is hardly made of such, and a relationship you root for opposite Colman’s emotionally twisty turn. “Wicker” threatens to feel largely like a logline writ into something grander (i.e., a short story with a wild idea stretched into a feature), but these actors are irresistibly weird and wonderful, as only they could be.

Grade: B

“Wicker” premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival.

article_text:
Ben Affleck is the latest celebrity to stick up for Tom Cruise ‘s “ Digger ” amid its disastrous box office run, but he’s doing so by warning moviegoers what exactly their trashing of the movie will result in. Mainly, publicly bashing “Digger” will only lead the major Hollywood studios to make “shitty” movies that don’t stand out from each other (aka more IP and franchise fare).

“It’s a little bit like the high-school bullying thing, with people who hadn’t even seen movies. You see it happening now, frankly, with ‘Digger,'” Affleck said. “Everybody wants to celebrate this bomb as if it’s the most exciting thing to happen. And you think like, it’s a pretty ambitious, interesting movie made by interesting people who have talent.”

“Everybody wants to count the money, what it lost or whatever. To me, I just think, if you punish movies that take risks, guess what you’re going to get? A bunch of shitty homogenized movies,” he continued. “You cannot do something interesting without taking a big swing. And that means you’re going to sometimes look bad.”

Affleck has weathered his own box office flops over the course of his decades-long career. “Digger,” from director Alejandro G. Iñárritu, stars Cruise as an oil tycoon who is faced with the end of the world after one of his rigs in Antartica malfunctions and sends ice caps hurtling towards Europe. The movie strongly divided critics (53% on Rotten Tomatoes) and has only earned $15 million at the domestic box office since opening Oct. 2. With a production budget north of $160 million and a marketing budget pegged at $100 million, “Digger” would need to earn $350 million just to break even in theaters. The latest report from Variety has “Digger” loosing Warner Bros. around $245 million, making it one of the most costly flops in studio history.

Amid the movie’s unfortunate box office run, various Hollywood celebrities and industry names have rallied around Cruise and the movie. Neil Young recently posted on his website that “Digger” is “the best film I have ever seen.”

“None of the reviews I have read describe this film adequately, in my opinion,” Young wrote. “They seem to miss the overall effect and most of them are negative. This film lives in a world of art. It is its own best review. Don’t read any other reviews and forget this one before you see ‘Digger.’ It cannot be seen as a Tom Cruise film – that would be misleading. I would describe it as a film of our times… I do not view this film as a commercial venture. Rather it is an artful film of our times. The things that are said in ‘Digger’ are a direct reflection of today’s political and social world. The film is so full of artful expression and radical change ups, that it may be too much to take in for those expecting a commercial film like we are used to today.”

Mandy Patinkin agrees with Young, as the “Homeland” star and Tony winner hailed Cruise’s latest as an “instant classic” and “one of the greatest pieces of film I have ever seen in my entire life,” adding: “This is an incredible piece of work. It puts the heart and soul back into the cinema. Everything we all love about cinema, this is it. Please, please, please, run! Don’t walk, run, and see this film.”

“I loved this brilliant movie. It’s smart and trippy and aggressive and funny and ambitious,” Hathaway wrote on Letterboxd . “It’s worth making the time see and decide for yourself what you make of it. For me? 10/10.”

Watch Affleck’s full interview on the “Happy Sad Confused” podcast in the video below.

article_text:
The movie business “needed Netflix to wake up” the industry, according to Edward Berger , but the Oscar-winning All Quiet on the Western Front director predicted it could be the Hollywood studios inspiring the streaming service in years to come.

Related Stories

Netflix Dismisses Dan Lin As Film Boss Before Peter Rice Arrives

Netflix Names Peter Rice As Chief Content Officer

Speaking today during a fireside chat at the MIA Market in Rome, Berger offered an assessment of how Netflix, which greenlit Oscar winner All Quiet , had impacted Hollywood with its global streaming model.

“The movie business needed Netflix to wake up,” he said. “They needed a real disruptor. They had probably become complacent and thought, ‘Okay, let’s do this because it was successful [before]’.”

Netflix last week underwent its largest round of layoffs since 2022 – around 1,000 – incidentally the same year World War II pic All Quiet released. With Paramount and Warner Bros. recently becoming one under the Skydance banner and David Ellison promising to make 30 films a year, the wheel could be turning the other way.

Watch on Deadline

Berger didn’t comment directly on the market, but noted: “Maybe we are now entering a period where the relationship works the other way around, with Netflix being inspired by the movie business. I think the two worlds are additive.”

Berger recalled how Sasha Bühler, Netflix’s Director of Film for German-speaking Europe at the time All Quiet was on the market, gave him a simple assessment of how the streamer would handle the film .

“She said, ‘If the movie’s great, we’ll support it. If it’s not, we won’t.’ That’s so scary, but I really love that,” he added.

Berger called his experience with All Quiet and Netflix “singularly great, with no stress at all.” He praised the streamer for giving “a considerable amount of money for a German film – money we could not have raised in that environment through local or international sales,” coming just as the Covid-19 outbreak was beginning. “Without that support, we might not have been able to make the movie,” he added.

The film ultimately won the Best International Film category at the 2023 Oscars. Bühler, who helmed it for Netflix, exited the streamer in August this year, as we revealed at the time.

How an Italian actor changed ‘ Conclave ‘

Conclave director Berger charmed a room of Italian delegates today at the MIA Market with a humorous tale from the set of the Oscar-nominated pic, which filmed in Rome. He and his team were searching for a male Italian actor over the age of 65 who spoke English. “The list was very short,” he recalled to laughs from the room.

Sergio Castellitto was recommended to play Cardinal Tedesco, and soon given the role. It quickly became clear that Castellitto’s English was limited, but this led to an unexpected change of direction for the movie.

Castellitto began changing lines from English into Italian, and with just days to go before filming, the decision was made to add the language. “We had an all-English cast and Sergio was speaking basically only Italian,” he laughed.

Ralph Fiennes, who was leading the cast as Cardinal Thomas Lawrence, then decided he would need to quickly learn Italian, so he could respond naturally. “No one was going to go and say, ‘We’re going to stop the film,'” said Berger.

It has been a busy few years for Berger, with another bustling period coming up. We were first with the news that Berger had given the World War Z sequel impetus by being attached as director, with Brad Pitt returning to star.

The original film, released in 2013, was based on Max Brooks’ bestselling 2006 novel World War Z: An Oral History of the Zombie War . Pitt, Dede Gardner and Jeremy Kleiner are producing the sequel on behalf of Plan B Entertainment. Berger will also executive produce. Dennis Kelly will write the script.

Berger is also attached to direct the untitled Lance Armstrong movie package starring Austin Butler as the disgraced cyclist, with Apple winning a heated auction . He will also direct Itamar Moses’ Netflix pic Stradivarius .

Berger is headlining this year’s MIA Market in Rome alongside the likes of Jane Tranter. The event begins today and runs through October 23.
